49567.etyen:
The lowercase form of S. Its modern rounded shape developed from cursive and minuscule forms of Latin S. In medieval and early modern writing, round ⟨s⟩ coexisted with long ⟨ſ⟩; long ⟨ſ⟩ was generally used initially and medially, while round ⟨s⟩ was normally used word-finally. The round form eventually became standard in all positions as long ⟨ſ⟩ fell out of general use around the beginning of the 19th century.
The Latin letter was adopted through Etruscan 𐌔 (s) from a western form of Ancient Greek Σ (S, “sigma”), ultimately from Phoenician 𐤔 (š, “šīn; tooth”). The Norwegian letter name ess ul / The uppercase form of s. From Latin S, through Etruscan 𐌔 (s), from a western form of Ancient Greek Σ (S, “sigma”), ultimately from Phoenician 𐤔 (š, “šīn; tooth”). The shape and alphabetic position of Greek sigma continue Phoenician šīn, whose sibilant sound was adapted to Greek /s/. The Greek name σίγμα (sígma, “sigma”) may have been influenced by Phoenician 𐤎 (s, “sāmek”), while the latter letter otherwise developed into Greek Ξ (X, “xi”). 1000351.etyen:
Borrowed from American English bingo (“bingo”), originally the cry used by a player upon winning. The English word is of uncertain origin, perhaps an extension of bing, an imitative word suggesting the ringing of a bell; compare the use of bingo! as an exclamation of sudden realization or success.

1000607.etyen:
Internationalism, based on Portuguese Portuguese São Tomé e Príncipe (“Saint Thomas and Prince”), with Portuguese e (“and”) replaced by Norwegian og (“and”). The name combines the names of the country's two principal islands, São Tomé (“Saint Thomas”) and Príncipe (“Prince”).
São Tomé (“Saint Thomas”) was named after Saint Thomas the Apostle because the island was reached by Portuguese navigators on Saint Thomas's feast day, 21 December. Portuguese São (“Saint”) is from Old Galician-Portuguese Old Galician-Portuguese san (“saint”), a shortened form of santo (“saint”), from Latin Latin sānctus

1004703.etyen:
From Othilie (“female given name”) + borg (“castle, fortress; place-name element”), with German-style genitive/linking -en-. The name comes from the farm Othilienborg gård, split off from Steindal nordre in 1847 and probably named after a female relative. The second element borg is from Old Norse borg (“fortress, castle”), from Proto-Germanic *burgz (“fortified settlement, stronghold”).
Compare similarly formed Trondheim place names such as Charlottenlund and Rosenborg.

1004959.etyen:
Borrowed from Dutch hartebeest (“hartebeest”), formed from Dutch hart (“hart, deer”), an alternative form of hert (“deer”), + beest (“animal, beast”), literally “deer beast”. Dutch hert is ultimately from Proto-Germanic *herutaz (“deer”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“horn”), while beest is from Middle Dutch beeste (“beast”), from Old French beste (“beast”), from Latin bēstia (“animal, beast”). Compare the parallel borrowings Danish hartebeest, Swedish hartbest and German Hartebeest (“hartebeest”).
